items.title: 4.4.1 Minor and Cofactor of an Element of a Matrix or its Determinant

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: A determinant of order 3 is worked out by breaking it into smaller determinants of order 2. The minor and the cofactor are the names of these smaller pieces. Learn them well: they are used for every determinant of order 3 (4.4.2) and again for the adjoint and inverse (4.5).

Let us consider a square matrix \(A\) of order \(n\), then the minor of an element \(a_{ij}\), denoted by \(M_{ij}\), is the determinant formed by deleting the \(i\)th row and the \(j\)th column of \(A\) (or \(|A|\)).
For example, consider a square matrix \(A\) of order 3,
To find the minor of the element \(a_{12}\), delete the first row and second column of \(A\); that is

blocks.alt: A 3 by 3 matrix with entries a11 to a33. A dashed horizontal line runs through the first row and a dashed vertical line through the second column: the row and column deleted to get the minor M12.
blocks.caption: Figure: deleting row 1 and column 2 of A leaves the minor M₁₂ (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How to read \(a_{ij}\): the first subscript \(i\) is the row, the second \(j\) is the column. So \(a_{12}\) sits in row 1, column 2, and to find \(M_{12}\) we cover row 1 and column 2.
Why delete exactly that row and column? Because they are the row and column that pass through the element itself. What is left is always a square block one size smaller: for order 3 every minor is a determinant of order 2, so a matrix of order 3 has 9 minors, one for each element.
The cofactor of an element \(a_{ij}\) of a square matrix \(A\), denoted by \(A_{ij}\), is defined by

blocks.text_alt: A sub i j equals minus one to the power i plus j, times M sub i j

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The factor \((-1)^{i+j}\) only decides a sign:
if \(i + j\) is even, \((-1)^{i+j} = +1\) and the cofactor equals the minor;
if \(i + j\) is odd, \((-1)^{i+j} = -1\) and the cofactor is the minor with its sign changed.
For order 3 the signs form a chessboard pattern, starting with \(+\) at the top left:

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Our own worked example (not from the book). Take
\[B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 4 & 5 \\ 1 & 0 & 6 \end{bmatrix}\]
Find the minors and cofactors of the elements of row 1.
\(M_{11}\): delete row 1 and column 1:
\[M_{11} = \begin{vmatrix} 4 & 5 \\ 0 & 6 \end{vmatrix} = 24 - 0 = 24\]
\(M_{12}\): delete row 1 and column 2:
\[M_{12} = \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 5 \\ 1 & 6 \end{vmatrix} = 0 - 5 = -5\]
\(M_{13}\): delete row 1 and column 3:
\[M_{13} = \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 4 \\ 1 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = 0 - 4 = -4\]
Cofactors (signs \(+, -, +\)):
\[B_{11} = (+1)(24) = 24\]
\[B_{12} = (-1)(-5) = 5\]
\[B_{13} = (+1)(-4) = -4\]
These are used again in 4.4.2, where this determinant is found to be 41.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Minor \(M_{ij}\): the determinant left after deleting row \(i\) and column \(j\).
2. Cofactor \(A_{ij} = (-1)^{i+j} M_{ij}\): the minor with a sign.
3. \(i + j\) even: cofactor = minor; \(i + j\) odd: cofactor = \(-\)minor.
4. Order 3 sign pattern: \(+ - +\), \(- + -\), \(+ - +\).
5. A matrix of order 3 has 9 minors and 9 cofactors, each a determinant of order 2 (with a sign).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Mixing up rows and columns: in \(a_{32}\) the row is 3 and the column is 2.
2. Giving the minor the sign: the minor has no extra sign; only the cofactor carries \((-1)^{i+j}\).
3. Double negatives: if \(M_{12} = -5\), then \(A_{12} = -(-5) = 5\), not \(-5\).
4. Using the same letter carelessly: \(a_{12}\) (small \(a\)) is an element, \(A_{12}\) (capital) is its cofactor.
